newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dresdner urges support for Frankfurt skyscraper.
newsitem.headline: Dresdner urges support for Frankfurt skyscraper.

text.p: Germany's Dresdner Bank AG on Wednesday appealed for support from city planners for its disputed proposal to fill in a gap on Frankfurt's famed skyline with a new skyscraper.

At a joint news conference with the city's Chamber of Industry and Commerce, the bank said delays over the project, sparked by quibbles on aesthetic and ecological grounds, sent out a bad signal about Frankfurt as a modern financial centre.

"Dresdner Bank remains open for dialogue but will have to orient its decisions on exisiting and future jobs in Frankfurt according to how we are accompanied on this project," board member Joachim von Harbou told a news conference.

The main sticking point with Dresdner's still-unfinalised plans is the projected height of the building, especially as it will be sited outside the traditional banking district which is home to the landmark twin glass towers of Deutsche Bank.

While likely to be dwarfed by Commerzbank's headquarters -- at 298.74 metres the city's newest, tallest and glitziest skyscraper -- the Dresdner building will be on the outskirts of Frankfurt's "Bahnhofsviertel", a seedy but developing cluster of streets radiating from the main railway station.

Planners in December decreed the building should be no higher than 115 metres, considerably smaller than the 165-metre building originally discussed and lower than a neighbouring skyscraper, which Dresdner says is 150 metres.
Dresdner argues that a tall building would raise fewer environmental and aesthetic problems than a shorter one.

The bank also insists it needs a large building to house the 1,600 administrative staff to be centred there and has in the past warned that these jobs may have to be relocated elsewhere -- a nightmare for promoters of Frankfurt.
While the bank will remain headquartered in its existing skyscraper, now being modernised, it wants to centralise more support staff in Frankfurt as well.
"Have no doubt that a lot of people in London, Amsterdam and Paris are going to be very happy about this dispute," said Frank Niethammer, president of Frankfurt's Chamber of Industry and Commerce.

While Frankfurt's status as a financial centre would get a much-needed boost from the decision to site the European Central Bank here, delays with building projects could deter a lot of potential investors in the city, Niethammer warned.

Frankfurt promoters are pround of the city's skyline, which mushroomed up over the past 10 years and prompted residents to rechristen the city "Mainhattan", after the river Main which runs through its centre.
The Commerzbank tower, designed by eminent architect Norman Foster, last year replaced the Trade Fair Tower or Messeturm as Frankfurt's -- and Europe's -- largest skyscraper.

Dresdner plans to present city planners with a proposal for its building, based on a competition between seven architects, six weeks from now. The bank aims to have completed the building in the year 2000.
